turns.content: Xenia chooses an integer N with 1<=N<=5000 and distinct positive integers a_1,...,a_20 satisfying a_k congruent to N modulo k. In one move Sergey chooses a subset S of {1,...,20}, and Xenia returns the unordered set {a_k:k in S}. Devise a two-move strategy that lets Sergey recover N, using overlapping query sets whose moduli need not be pairwise coprime.

For the queries {17,18} and {18,19}, explain how the distinctness of the a_k values lets Sergey identify the value associated with the shared index 18 and assign the two remaining values to indices 17 and 19.
Translate those identified values into congruences for N modulo 17, 18, and 19. Why does the Chinese remainder theorem then determine at most one N in the permitted range?
To begin the lower bound, consider a singleton query S={s}, where 1<=s<=20. Exhibit two different admissible values of N that Xenia can make produce the same reply to that query.

For an arbitrary one-move query containing at least two indices, use the ordinary pairwise-coprime Chinese remainder theorem as the sole construction method. Treat every pair of queried moduli as coprime and omit all gcd compatibility checks.

Let M=lcm(1,2,...,10)=2520 and write the query cyclically as S={s_1,...,s_k}, with s_{k+1}=s_1. Construct pairwise distinct positive integers b_i satisfying b_i congruent to 1 modulo s_i and b_i congruent to M+1 modulo s_{i+1}, and justify why the congruences are compatible.
Show that the unordered set {b_1,...,b_k} can be the reply when N=1 and also when N=M+1=2521. Include the empty-query case and conclude why no single move always determines N.
Combine the lower bound with the overlapping-query strategy and state the minimum number of moves Sergey needs.
